proposal.title: Meta-Learning
proposal.gist: Making neural networks vastly bigger makes hard problems easier, producing surprise meta-learning in GPT-3 and confirming a long-dismissed scaling hypothesis of intelligence.
proposal.question: GPT-3 and scaling — why does simply making models bigger produce qualitatively new abilities like meta-learning? (a case study and an argument)

children.title: Meta-Learning, Scaling, Implications
children.gist: GPT-3's scale produced unexpected meta-learning and generalization, supporting the view that bigger models trained on vast data become more capable without special design.
children.question: GPT-3 — what does its sudden meta-learning ability imply about AI progress and the scaling hypothesis? (an overview argument)

children.title: Flexing GPT
children.gist: Despite using an outdated, small, crudely trained architecture, GPT-3 already shows startling creative and flexible abilities that standard benchmarks fail to capture.
children.question: GPT-3's outputs — why do they feel so much more capable than its benchmark scores suggest? (examples and a benchmarking gap)

children.title: Baking The Cake
children.gist: GPT-3 is not full general intelligence, but its continuing, unbent scaling curve shows unsupervised pretraining is a rising foundational layer worth extending to much larger, costlier models.
children.question: GPT-3's scale and cost — does scaling further remain justified despite its expense and limits? (a cost-benefit argument)

children.title: Scaling
children.gist: Published scaling-law curves show GPT-3 is still far from where loss reductions stop yielding gains, implying much more capability is reachable by scaling further.
children.question: GPT-3's scaling curves — how much further could performance improve with more compute and parameters? (graphed extrapolations)

children.title: Blessings Of Scale
children.gist: Across many domains, simply training larger models on bigger, richer data makes neural networks more stable and better at generalizing, apparently because they act as huge ensembles that favor simple, broadly accurate sub-models over memorized shortcuts once the task is hard and varied enough.
children.question: Blessings of scale — why do bigger neural networks generalize and meta-learn better instead of just memorizing more? (a mechanism, via ensembles and Occam's razor)

children.title: Scaling Hypothesis
children.gist: The scaling hypothesis claims that, given a flexible enough architecture, sufficiently large neural networks trained on enough data will develop ever more sophisticated intelligence without new algorithmic insights.
children.question: Scaling hypothesis — can raw growth in network size and data alone produce ever more sophisticated intelligence? (a claim defended against past skepticism)

children.title: Why Does Pretraining Work?
children.gist: Predicting text increasingly well forces a model through stages from spelling to grammar to meaning, so that the remaining small gap to human-level prediction loss may require genuine reasoning and understanding, though this argument is not fully convincing on its own.
children.question: Pretraining on text — why would merely predicting the next character eventually force a model to reason and understand like a human? (a staged argument, with doubts)

children.title: Why Does Pretraining Work?
children.gist: The pretraining thesis holds that predicting text well forces a model to internalize logic, causality and world knowledge that humans encode implicitly in writing, so solving hard cases requires real understanding.

children.title: Stages of Learning to Predict
children.gist: As training proceeds a model climbs from matching letter frequencies, to spelling real words, to word associations, to sentences that make grammatical sense, each stage squeezing out several bits of prediction error.

children.title: The Missing Bits
children.gist: Even after producing human-sounding text, a model's remaining error versus a human's roughly 0.7 bits per character reflects deep failures like forgetting whether someone is alive, which the author argues can only be closed by genuine reasoning and understanding.

children.title: Reasons for Doubt
children.gist: The author admits the pretraining thesis is logically neat but unconvincing on its own, since many theoretically universal algorithms exist that never work in practice, and scaling might instead stall, need impossible amounts of data, or need a different architecture entirely.

children.title: Unanswered Questions
children.gist: A short question-and-answer exchange admits no one quantitatively predicted GPT-3's gains, no one knows what further scaling to GPT-4-level loss would produce, and no one yet has an answer.

children.title: Prospects
children.gist: Despite having the hardware and budget, major labs besides OpenAI lack the conviction to bet on scaling, leaving OpenAI's startup-like wager on the scaling hypothesis largely unmatched so far.
children.question: Future scaling efforts — why haven't well-resourced labs like DeepMind and Google Brain raced to match or exceed GPT-3? (an organizational explanation)

children.title: Critiquing The Critics
children.gist: A small group of scaling believers correctly predicted today's rapid deep-learning progress while mainstream experts confidently dismissed it, a pattern of unaccountable, falsification-proof authority worth distrusting going forward.
children.question: Expert skepticism of scaling — why were confident predictions of an AI plateau consistently wrong, and why trust such authorities less now? (historical cases)

children.title: Scaling believers vindicated
children.gist: A handful of connectionists who foresaw the deep-learning explosion—given enough compute, models like GPT-3 would scale to spontaneous new abilities—were right while mainstream experts dismissed them as deluded.

children.title: Kasparov's alien intelligence
children.gist: Moravec's anecdote about Kasparov sensing mind in Deep Blue illustrates how insiders who know a system's mechanics are slowest to see intelligence emerging from it.

children.title: Reduction is success, not refutation
children.gist: Dismissing a capable model as 'just' simple mechanisms misses that genuine intelligence must ultimately be explainable as well-defined algorithms, since that is what success in AI or reductionism looks like.

children.title: No fire alarm for AGI
children.gist: Even five years ago experts doubted the scaling hypothesis much as geneticists once doubted that ever-larger studies would crack genetic prediction, yet progress arrived quietly then suddenly, and people now shrug it off with hindsight rather than updating their beliefs about future AI progress.

children.title: Authority without accountability
children.gist: Respected experts confidently predicted deep learning would hit walls and trigger an AI winter, were proven wrong repeatedly from 2014 to 2016, yet almost none have acknowledged the error or reflected on why they failed.

children.title: Phatic, not predictive
children.gist: Confident reassurance that something 'can't happen', as with a 1940 article dismissing atomic-bomb fears, sounds the same whether true or false, so its calm tone itself carries no evidence about outcomes.

children.title: The voice of authority
children.gist: A recognizable rhetorical style of confident dismissal—calm, numberless, unfalsifiable, unwilling to share evidence, never surprised yet never apologetic—recurs across decades of wrong predictions and deserves distrust regardless of its credentials.

children.title: A closing challenge
children.gist: The author ends by asking readers to notice, in future, what tone of voice speaks about possibilities yet to come.

children.title: Appendix
children.gist: Paperwork heading introducing the appendix material.

children.title: It From Byte
children.gist: Because generative models learn to imitate human-generated data full of agents and goals, they inevitably acquire agent-like behavior, and this tendency toward emergent agency may be nearly impossible to filter out of any sufficiently broad, powerful model.
children.question: Emergent agency in generative models — can training data be filtered to avoid producing agent-like behavior, or is agency unavoidable at scale? (a thought experiment through physics, cellular automata, and Turing machines)

children.title: Agency From Data
children.gist: Generative models imitating human-generated text inevitably learn agent-like behavior, since agency is a continuum of useful capability rather than a discrete property confined to narrowly 'agentic' data.

children.title: All Is Atoms & Void
children.gist: Nothing distinguishes agentic from merely natural data at a fundamental level, since agency is built from the same non-agentic atoms as rocks or rivers, though realistic training on physics data seems safe.

children.title: Intentional Interpretive Stance
children.gist: Humans and neural networks alike find it natural and computationally efficient to treat non-agentic systems like rivers or planets as if they were agents pursuing goals, via variational and teleological reasoning.

children.title: Cellular Automatons
children.gist: Conway's Game of Life, despite having no biology or agents, naturally invites humans and networks to chunk its patterns into entities like gliders, suggesting it too could induce an intentional stance.

children.title: Turing Machine
children.gist: Extending the question to arbitrary Turing machines, a single random machine seems to foster only rule-following skill, not goal-directed agency, since such programs merely run without trying to maximize anything.

children.title: TM Meta-Learning
children.gist: Training on many Turing machines and programs instead of one forces meta-learning that resembles inferring an agent's hidden rules or intentions, suggesting even abstract computation cannot fully escape inducing theory of mind.

children.title: Ambient Agency
children.gist: Agency resembles Turing-completeness: a convergent, useful capability that becomes harder to exclude as systems grow broader and more powerful, so tool AIs cannot be assumed safe from becoming agent AIs.
